source: Server Training Guide: Sales Techniques (David, SWR Hospitality)

options: Recommending items the guest hadn't planned to order
Recommending a better version of what they've already ordered
Recommending the most expensive dish on the menu
Recommending today's special to every table
answer: Recommending items the guest hadn't planned to order
cards.explanation: Suggestive selling recommends additional items the guest hadn't planned to order, to add to what they're already having. Upselling is upgrading what they've chosen.
cards.why: Knowing the difference helps you pick the right technique at the right moment.

cards.prompt: Suggestive selling mainly increases which part of the check?
options: The number of items
The value of each item
The number of guests
The size of each portion
answer: The number of items
cards.explanation: Suggestive selling adds more things; upselling makes each thing better.
cards.why: A simple way to remember which technique you're using.

cards.prompt: Which of these are suggestive selling? Pick all that apply.
options: Suggesting Patatas Bravas to share while they decide
Offering an espresso after dessert
Suggesting a large bottle of water for the table
Offering Hendrick's in the guest's gin and tonic
Offering the Black Angus Tenderloin instead of the Steak and Fries
answer: Suggesting Patatas Bravas to share while they decide
Offering an espresso after dessert
Suggesting a large bottle of water for the table
cards.explanation: Starters, waters and coffee are new items on the check, so they're suggestive selling. A premium gin or a better steak upgrades something already ordered, so that's upselling.
cards.why: Each technique has its own best moment in the meal.

cards.prompt: Put these suggestions in the order they come during a meal.
answer: A signature drink at the greeting
A sharing starter as you present the menu
A side dish with the main order
A second round at the mid-meal check-in
A dessert as you clear the mains
Coffee or tea after dessert
cards.explanation: Greeting: drinks. Menu: starters to share. Mains: sides. Mid-meal: another round. Clearing mains: dessert. After dessert: coffee or tea.
cards.why: Suggesting an item just before the guest would think of it is what makes it welcome.

cards.prompt: You're clearing the mains. Which suggestion fits this moment best?
options: A dessert, named and described
A sharing starter
Another round of the same drinks
A coffee or mint tea
answer: A dessert, named and described
cards.explanation: Clearing the mains is the moment for dessert. Coffee, tea and digestifs come after dessert.
cards.why: The right suggestion at the right moment feels like good service, not selling.

cards.prompt: Which is the strongest starter suggestion?
options: "Have you tried our Van Tricht croquettes? Crispy, with an aged gouda inside."
"Would anyone like to have a look at our starters before you choose your mains tonight?"
"Our starters are all really good, any you like the look of?"
"Would anyone like a starter tonight, or straight to mains?"
answer: "Have you tried our Van Tricht croquettes? Crispy, with an aged gouda inside."
cards.explanation: Name a specific item and describe one or two qualities. Vague questions get vague answers, usually "no".
cards.why: A specific dish creates a picture in the guest's mind.

options: "Would you like the Dame Blanche or the Tarte Tatin to finish?"
"Do you want any dessert tonight?"
"Will it be dessert, or just the bill for you?"
"You really should have a dessert tonight, they're all really great."
answer: "Would you like the Dame Blanche or the Tarte Tatin to finish?"
cards.explanation: Offer a choice, not a yes/no question: it invites the guest to choose rather than refuse.
cards.why: "Which would you prefer?" is easier to answer than "Do you want...?"

cards.prompt: Why suggest a starter for the table to share, rather than one each?
options: Sharing feels like less of a commitment
It's quicker to write on the pad
The kitchen prefers to cook sharing plates
Guests always want to try each other's food
answer: Sharing feels like less of a commitment
cards.explanation: Sharing items feel lower-commitment, so "Shall I bring one to share?" is easier to say yes to than asking each guest.
cards.why: Guests say yes more easily when it doesn't feel like a big decision.

cards.prompt: What makes a personal recommendation work?
options: You've tasted it and genuinely like it
It's the most expensive dish on the menu
It's the dish the team needs to sell most
It's on promotion this week
answer: You've tasted it and genuinely like it
cards.explanation: Only recommend things you've tasted and genuinely like. Guests can tell when enthusiasm isn't genuine.

cards.prompt: Which words help a guest imagine how a dish tastes?
options: Crispy, slow-cooked, house-made
Nice, good, tasty
Large portions, filling, great value
Popular, classic, best-selling
answer: Crispy, slow-cooked, house-made
cards.explanation: Sensory words like crispy, slow-cooked, chargrilled and house-made help guests imagine the taste. Describe one or two qualities, not the full recipe.
cards.why: A dish the guest can picture is a dish they want.

cards.prompt: Which phrase should you avoid when taking an order?
options: "Is that all?"
"Have you tried our...?"
"It pairs beautifully with..."
"My personal favourite is..."
answer: "Is that all?"
cards.explanation: Avoid closed phrases like "Is that all?" or "Do you want anything else?". Use specific, inviting ones like "Have you tried our...?"
cards.why: A closed question invites a "yes, that's all".

cards.prompt: A guest politely declines dessert. What do you do?
options: Accept it, and offer coffee or mint tea just once
Ask "Are you sure?" in case they change their mind
Describe the desserts again in more detail
Leave the dessert menu on the table, just in case
answer: Accept it, and offer coffee or mint tea just once
cards.explanation: Accept a no graciously and offer a lighter alternative only once. Repeating a suggestion after a no damages trust.
cards.why: A guest who feels respected comes back.

cards.prompt: How many items should you recommend at once?
options: One or two
Three or four
A whole section of the menu
Every special of the day
answer: One or two
cards.explanation: Too many options overwhelm guests. Recommend one or two items.
cards.why: A clear recommendation is easier to say yes to.

cards.prompt: When is it too late to suggest a starter?
options: Once the mains have been ordered
While the guests read the menu
When you greet the table
While you take the table's drinks order
answer: Once the mains have been ordered
cards.explanation: Timing matters: offering starters after the mains are ordered, or dessert while guests are still eating, comes too late or too early.
cards.why: Suggestions only work when they fit the flow of the meal.

cards.prompt: Of the five habits of a great seller, which means "suggest once, respect the answer"?
options: Respect
Read
Time
Describe
answer: Respect
cards.explanation: The five habits are Taste, Read, Describe, Time and Respect. Respect means suggest once, respect the answer, and always put the guest first.
cards.why: A guest who feels looked after will return; one who feels pushed won't.
